extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the stylistic features, thematic preoccupations, and narrative techniques characteristic of Chinua Achebe's fiction (how he writes and what his works typically emphasize). Useful for literary analysis or emulating Achebe-like writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of Achebe's fiction draws heavily on the oral tradition of the Igbo people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He incorporates folk tales into his stories, exposing community values in both content and form; e.g., the Earth and Sky tale in Things Fall Apart which emphasises interdependency of masculine and feminine. This oral-rooted approach shapes narrative voice and cultural framing across his novels and short stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proverbs and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe uses proverbs throughout his narratives, repeating points made in conversation to convey values and communal judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic Anjali Gera notes the use of proverbs in Arrow of God 'serves to create through an echo effect the judgement of a community upon an individual violation.' Repetition creates communal voice and moral emphasis; the technique is applied differently across works (see variation between rural and urban novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate choice of English as medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe chooses English to communicate across Nigeria and to reach international readers, seeing it as 'the one central language enjoying nationwide currency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using English allowed his books to be read in colonial ruling nations and to reach a broad Nigerian readership; the choice is framed as pragmatic and strategic rather than a simple adoption of the coloniser's tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending and adapting English to African thought
rubrics_metrics.description: He argues writers can either contain their ideas within conventional English or push back its limits to accommodate African modes of thought, and advocates extending the frontiers of English through mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: expand syntax, usage, and idiom deliberately rather than naively; Achebe references James Baldwin's struggle as a precedent. Practically this manifests as altered syntax, repetition of Igbo ideas in English, and narrative asides integrated into descriptive sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic and idiomatic transformation to create a distinct African style
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe alters syntax, usage and idiom to transform English into a distinctly African style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include repetition of an Igbo idea in standard English, narrative asides inside descriptive sentences, and other micro-level adjustments to convey cultural concepts without losing readability. These choices are presented as craft decisions to accommodate cultural specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centering indigenous life (Igbo culture) rather than using it as background
rubrics_metrics.description: Depiction of the Igbo culture itself is paramount; Achebe 'seeks to produce the effect of a precolonial reality as an Igbo-centric response to a Eurocentrically constructed imperial "reality".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indigenous life functions as the principal subject and interpretive frame, not mere setting. Portrayals of customs, worldview, and community institutions are integral to theme and plot (e.g., Things Fall Apart, Arrow of God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme: tradition versus colonial modernity
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevalent theme is the intersection of African tradition (particularly Igbo varieties) and modernity, especially as embodied by European colonialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict how contact with missionaries, colonial institutions, and urban offices creates internal divisions, corrodes traditional structures or invites corruption (examples: Umuofia in Things Fall Apart; Obi in No Longer at Ease). Address both individual and institutional vectors of colonial impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic endings with communal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'standard Achebean ending' often results in the destruction of an individual, which leads to the downfall or crisis of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achebe's tragic outcomes echo classical tragedy (Sophocles, Shakespeare) but are not presented as fatalistic inevitabilities; the individual's fall symbolises broader postcolonial crisis. Use tragedy to link personal failure with social/cultural consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral complexity and rejection of absolutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe seeks to portray neither moral absolutes nor fatalistic inevitability; he asserts 'no single truth satisfied me' and resists simplistic binaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters and actions should be shown as morally complex—'evil is never all evil; goodness on the other hand is often tainted with selfishness.' Avoid didactic moralising; present competing truths and the need for compromise or synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of gender roles: masculinity and femininity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender roles and society's conceptions of masculinity and femininity are frequent themes; Achebe depicts patriarchal Igbo society, male violence and the valuation of women largely via motherhood, but also includes nuanced female figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some critics call Achebe sexist for uncritical depictions, others argue he represents limited character perspectives or uses exaggerated binaries to render history recognisable to international readers. Readings through womanist lenses emphasise resistance, dignity, and the 'mother within' (e.g., Ekwefi and Ezinma's relationship). Use gender portrayals to explore social values and tensions rather than endorse them uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short stories' moral focus influenced by folk tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe's short stories are heavily influenced by the oral tradition and often have morals emphasising the importance of cultural traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Achebe considered his short stories a 'pretty lean harvest' compared to novels, they nonetheless employ folk-tale-derived morals and community-focused lessons; use compact narrative and moral emphasis when working in short form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of oral/repetitive techniques by setting (rural vs urban)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deployment of oral devices (proverbs, repetition) varies by context: the use of such repetition in Achebe's urban novels (No Longer at Ease, A Man of the People) is less pronounced than in his rural-set works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the density of oral-tradition techniques depending on setting and thematic needs—rural, community-centered stories call for stronger oral features; urban/modern contexts may demand subtler incorporation.
